title: Strattera and Alcohol: Liver Risk, Side Effects, and Safe Limits
excerpt: Can you drink on Strattera? How atomoxetine and alcohol overlap on your liver, heart, side effects, and mood, why skipping doses doesn't help, and when to see a doctor.
metaDescription: Can you drink on Strattera? How atomoxetine and alcohol affect your liver, heart, and mood, why skipping doses doesn't help, and warning signs to know.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** Strattera (atomoxetine) and alcohol don't have a dramatic, dangerous chemical reaction the way some medicines do, and an occasional drink is something many prescribers are willing to discuss with patients. But the combination isn't risk-free. Strattera carries a warning about rare but serious liver injury, it can raise your heart rate and blood pressure, and it often causes nausea, dizziness, and either sleepiness or trouble sleeping. Alcohol pushes on every one of those. The drug's label advises caution with alcohol, and the safest choice is to drink lightly if at all, and to talk it through with the person who prescribed it.

**The quick rules:** Don't skip your Strattera dose to "make room" for drinking; it doesn't work that way and it can set your treatment back. If you do drink, keep it to one or two drinks, eat first, and pace yourself, especially in the first few weeks on the drug or after a dose change. Don't drink at all if you've been told your liver enzymes are high, you have liver disease, or you've had dark urine, yellow eyes, or pain under your right ribs. And if your mood has been low, alcohol is the wrong tool; tell your prescriber instead.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and the drug's prescribing information. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history and the rest of your medication list. **Talk to your doctor before drinking on Strattera if** you have liver disease or a history of high liver enzymes, high blood pressure or a heart condition, depression or thoughts of self-harm, or you take other medicines (especially antidepressants like fluoxetine, paroxetine, or bupropion). **Get medical help promptly if** you notice yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, itching all over, pain under the right ribs, or unexplained flu-like symptoms; chest pain, fainting, or a racing heartbeat that won't settle; or any thoughts of harming yourself. In an emergency, call 911 (US), or call or text 988 for the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline.

## What Strattera Is, and Why It's Different From Adderall

Strattera is the brand name for **atomoxetine**, a prescription medicine for ADHD in children, teens, and adults. Most ADHD medicines, such as Adderall, Vyvanse, and Ritalin, are stimulants. Strattera is not. It belongs to a class called **selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors**, which in plain words means it keeps more of the brain chemical norepinephrine (noradrenaline) available in the parts of the brain that handle attention, planning, and impulse control.

That difference matters for alcohol in a few ways:

- **It isn't a controlled substance.** Stimulants are tightly regulated because of their misuse potential. Strattera isn't, because it doesn't produce a "high" or a rush.
- **It works steadily, not dose by dose.** A stimulant kicks in within an hour and wears off within the day. Strattera builds up over several weeks of daily use, and its benefit depends on taking it consistently. You can't really "take a day off" for a party without losing some of that steady effect.
- **It doesn't mask drunkenness the way stimulants do.** The biggest worry with [Adderall and alcohol](/never-hungover/adderall-and-alcohol) is that the stimulant makes you feel more sober than you are, so you overdrink. Strattera doesn't have that strong wake-promoting push. In fact, the prescribing information notes that in a study, drinking alcohol alongside atomoxetine didn't change alcohol's intoxicating effects.

So if you've read scary articles about stimulants and drinking, not all of that applies here. The concerns with Strattera are different, and they're mostly about your liver, your heart and blood pressure, side effects that stack, and your mood.

## The Real Interaction: Four Places Strattera and Alcohol Overlap

There isn't one single mechanism that makes Strattera and alcohol clash. Instead, there are four areas where they push in the same direction.

### 1. Your liver

Strattera's prescribing information includes a warning about **severe liver injury**. It's rare. Reports after the drug came to market described a small number of patients who developed liver damage, in a few cases serious. The label tells doctors to stop the drug in anyone who develops jaundice (yellowing) or lab evidence of liver injury, and not to restart it.

Atomoxetine is broken down in the liver, mainly by an enzyme called **CYP2D6**. Alcohol is also processed in the liver, through a different set of enzymes. The two don't directly compete for the same enzyme, so the concern isn't that alcohol makes atomoxetine levels spike. The concern is simpler: if your liver is already under strain from regular heavy drinking or fatty liver, you have less margin if a rare drug reaction does occur, and alcohol-related liver irritation can muddy the picture when your doctor is trying to work out what's going on.

That's why the liver is the headline issue on this page. One drink won't harm a healthy liver. Regular heavy drinking on top of a medicine with a liver warning is a different story.

### 2. Heart rate and blood pressure

Because Strattera raises norepinephrine, it tends to nudge **heart rate and blood pressure** up a little. For most people the change is modest, but the label tells doctors to measure both before starting and to keep checking.

Alcohol does its own thing to your cardiovascular system. In the moment, it widens blood vessels, which can make you flushed and sometimes lightheaded. Over the following hours and into the next day, many people notice a faster pulse, and heavy drinking is a well-known contributor to raised blood pressure over time. If you've ever felt your [heart racing after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking), you've felt this.

Put the two together and a heavy night can leave your heart working harder than either would alone. If you have high blood pressure, a heart rhythm problem, or a structural heart condition, this is worth a direct conversation with your doctor.

### 3. Side effects that stack

Strattera's most common side effects include **nausea, upset stomach, reduced appetite, dizziness, tiredness or sleepiness, and trouble sleeping**. The label also notes that some people get dizzy or faint when they stand up quickly, because of a drop in blood pressure on standing.

Alcohol causes nausea, dizziness, drowsiness, and broken sleep too. When both are in play, the effects can add up:

- **Nausea and stomach upset** may be worse, especially if you drank on an empty stomach (and Strattera can make you less hungry).
- **Dizziness and lightheadedness** can be more pronounced, raising the risk of a fall, particularly when you stand up suddenly.
- **Sleep** is the wild card. Some people feel sleepy on Strattera, and alcohol is sedating at first, so that combination can make you drowsier than expected. Others find Strattera makes it harder to sleep, and alcohol disrupts the second half of the night. Either way, you're unlikely to wake up rested. Our guide on [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) explains the alcohol side of that.

### 4. Mood

Strattera carries a **boxed warning** (the FDA's strongest kind) about an increased risk of suicidal thoughts in children and teenagers, based on clinical trials. Doctors are asked to watch closely for mood changes, especially in the first few months and after dose changes. Adults should also tell their prescriber about any worsening mood.

Alcohol is a depressant. It can lift your mood for an hour, but it often leaves people lower, more anxious, and more impulsive afterward. If you're in the early weeks of a new medicine that needs mood monitoring, alcohol makes it harder for you and your doctor to tell what's the drug, what's the drink, and what's you. If you've noticed you feel noticeably down or on edge the day after drinking, our piece on [alcohol and anxiety](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-anxiety-breaking-the-cycle-naturally-2025) covers why.

## Strattera and Liver Damage: The Signs to Know

Because the liver is the most serious concern, it's worth knowing what liver trouble looks like. According to the prescribing information, warning signs that should prompt a call to your doctor include:

- **Itching** all over without an obvious cause
- **Dark urine**
- **Yellowing of the skin or the whites of the eyes** (jaundice)
- **Pain or tenderness in the upper right part of the belly**, under the ribs
- **Unexplained flu-like symptoms**, such as tiredness, nausea, and loss of appetite

Some of those look a lot like a bad hangover, and that's exactly the problem. If you've been drinking, it's tempting to write off nausea and fatigue as "just the night before." Here's a useful rule: a hangover gets better within a day. If nausea, tiredness, or right-sided belly pain hangs around for more than a day or two, or if you see dark urine or yellow eyes at any point, don't wait it out. Call your prescriber, and get seen the same day if you have yellowing.

Your doctor can check your liver with a simple blood test. Routine liver tests aren't generally required for everyone on Strattera, but they're the right move if any of these signs show up, and it helps to be honest with your doctor about how much you drink so they can interpret the results.

## Can You Drink on Strattera? What Moderate Drinking Looks Like

There's no official "safe number" of drinks on Strattera, and anyone who gives you a precise figure that applies to everyone is guessing. The label urges caution rather than setting a limit. That said, here's how many prescribers and pharmacists tend to frame it:

| Situation | General guidance |
|---|---|
| Healthy adult, stable on Strattera for a while, no liver or heart issues | Light, occasional drinking (one or two drinks) may be acceptable. Ask your prescriber what's reasonable for you. |
| First few weeks on Strattera, or just after a dose increase | Better to avoid alcohol or keep it minimal until you know how the drug affects you. |
| High blood pressure, heart condition, or fainting episodes | Talk to your doctor before drinking at all. |
| Liver disease, high liver enzymes, or any past liver reaction | Avoid alcohol and discuss with your doctor. |
| Low mood, depression, or thoughts of self-harm | Avoid alcohol and tell your prescriber about your mood. |
| Under 21 (US) | Alcohol isn't legal, and teens on Strattera need extra mood monitoring. |

If your doctor is fine with occasional light drinking, a few habits make it gentler on your body:

- **Eat a real meal first.** Strattera can blunt appetite, and drinking on an empty stomach makes both nausea and dizziness worse.
- **Alternate with water.** Dehydration makes lightheadedness and a fast pulse more likely.
- **Go slow.** Your body clears roughly one standard drink per hour, though this varies a lot between people.
- **Stand up slowly**, especially late in the evening.
- **Skip binge sessions.** Several drinks in a short period is where the cardiovascular and liver concerns stack up most.

## Should You Skip Your Strattera Dose to Drink?

This is one of the most common questions, and the answer is generally **no**.

With a stimulant, people sometimes skip a dose because the drug wears off in hours and the main risk is having both in your system at once. Strattera doesn't work that way. Its benefit comes from steady, daily use. Atomoxetine's half-life (the time it takes for half of it to leave your body) is roughly five hours in most people, but it can be around a day in people whose bodies process it slowly, and its effect on ADHD symptoms depends on consistent levels over weeks.

Skipping one dose won't clear the drug's influence from your system, so it doesn't make drinking meaningfully "safer." What it can do is make your ADHD symptoms less controlled for a day or two, and if skipping becomes a habit, it can make the medicine look less effective than it really is. Strattera isn't known for a dangerous withdrawal effect, but you still shouldn't stop or start it on your own schedule.

If you know a big event is coming up, the better move is to talk to your prescriber ahead of time. They know your dose, your timing, and your history, and they can tell you what makes sense.

## Strattera vs. Stimulants and Alcohol: A Side-by-Side

If you've switched from a stimulant or you're weighing options, here's how the alcohol concerns compare in general terms:

| | Strattera (atomoxetine) | Stimulants (Adderall, Vyvanse, Ritalin) |
|---|---|---|
| Drug type | Non-stimulant (norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor) | Stimulant |
| Controlled substance | No | Yes |
| Masks how drunk you feel | Not to the same degree | Yes, a major reason people overdrink |
| Main alcohol concern | Liver warning, blood pressure and heart rate, stacked side effects, mood | Overdrinking, heart strain, next-day crash |
| Dose timing | Daily and steady; skipping doesn't help | Short-acting; timing matters more |
| Next day | Nausea, poor sleep, low mood possible | Crash, exhaustion, low mood common |

Neither column is a green light. Strattera's alcohol risks are different from stimulants', not absent. For the stimulant side of the comparison, see our guides on [Adderall and alcohol](/never-hungover/adderall-and-alcohol) and [Vyvanse and alcohol](/never-hungover/vyvanse-and-alcohol).

## Other Medicines That Change the Picture

Atomoxetine levels in your blood depend heavily on the CYP2D6 enzyme. Some common medicines block that enzyme and can raise atomoxetine levels significantly, which can make side effects like a fast heart rate, nausea, and dizziness stronger. The prescribing information names strong CYP2D6 blockers such as **fluoxetine (Prozac)**, **paroxetine (Paxil)**, and **quinidine**, and doctors often lower the Strattera dose when they're combined. **Bupropion (Wellbutrin)** also blocks this enzyme.

This matters for drinking because higher atomoxetine levels plus alcohol means more of the stacked side effects described above. If you take an antidepressant alongside Strattera, ask your pharmacist how the combination fits with alcohol. Our page on [Wellbutrin and alcohol](/never-hungover/wellbutrin-and-alcohol) covers its own separate alcohol concern, a lowered seizure threshold.

A few other combinations deserve a heads-up:

- **Decongestants and some asthma inhalers** (such as albuterol taken in large amounts, or pseudoephedrine) can add to the rise in heart rate and blood pressure.
- **MAO inhibitors** must never be combined with Strattera; the label is explicit about that.
- **Sleep aids and other sedating medicines** can make the drowsy effect of alcohol stronger.

For a broader look at how common medicines interact with alcohol and supplements, see our [medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025).

## What a Strattera Hangover Feels Like (and How to Ease It)

There's no special "Strattera hangover," but people on atomoxetine often report that hangovers feel worse than they used to. That makes sense: nausea, poor sleep, dizziness, and low appetite are already on the side-effect list, and a hangover brings all four.

If you wake up rough after drinking on Strattera:

- **Take your usual dose at your usual time**, with food, unless your doctor has told you otherwise. Food helps with the nausea.
- **Rehydrate steadily** with water or an electrolyte drink rather than gulping a large amount at once.
- **Eat something bland** like toast, rice, or a banana, even if your appetite is low.
- **Be careful with pain relievers.** Acetaminophen (Tylenol) is also processed by the liver, so keep to a single standard dose after drinking. Ibuprofen is easier on the liver but harder on the stomach.
- **Skip the extra coffee or energy drinks** if your heart already feels fast.
- **Watch for anything that lasts.** Normal hangover symptoms fade within a day. Persistent nausea, right-sided belly pain, dark urine, or yellow eyes are not a hangover; call your doctor.

## When to See a Doctor

> **Call your doctor promptly or get same-day care if** you have yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, itching all over, pain under the right ribs, or flu-like symptoms that don't clear within a day or two. **Call 911 or go to the emergency room if** you have chest pain, fainting, a very fast or irregular heartbeat that won't settle, severe confusion, or signs of severe alcohol poisoning (vomiting while drowsy, slow or irregular breathing, can't be woken, blue-tinged lips). **If you're having thoughts of harming yourself**, call or text 988 (US) or go to the nearest emergency room now.

It's also worth booking a regular appointment if you're finding it hard to stay within the limits you and your doctor agreed on, or if you notice you're drinking more since starting Strattera. Your prescriber has seen this before, and being honest helps them choose the right treatment and dose for you.

## Supporting Your Liver If You Choose to Drink

The most effective way to protect your liver on Strattera is the plain one: **drink less, drink slower, and eat and hydrate properly.** Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.

Some people also look at supplements. Here's an honest view, with one important rule up front: **check with your prescriber or pharmacist before adding any supplement to a prescription medicine**, especially one with a liver warning.

- **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of that research is in animals and lab settings, with limited human data. It's promising, but there is no good evidence that it reduces Strattera's liver risk, and it doesn't change any of the advice on this page. Its interactions with atomoxetine haven't been studied, so ask first. If your doctor is comfortable with it, a popular, well-reviewed option is [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), and a budget-friendly pick is [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people typically take and when.
- **Milk thistle and NAC** are other common liver-support supplements, with mixed human evidence. Our [best liver supplements guide](/never-hungover/best-liver-supplements) compares the options and what the research actually shows.

No supplement is a substitute for the liver warning signs above or for your doctor's blood tests.

## The Bottom Line

- Strattera is a non-stimulant ADHD medicine, so it doesn't mask drunkenness the way Adderall can, but that doesn't make alcohol risk-free.
- The main concerns are a **rare but serious liver warning**, **higher heart rate and blood pressure**, **stacked side effects** like nausea, dizziness, and poor sleep, and **mood changes**.
- If your doctor is fine with it, keep drinking light and occasional, eat first, hydrate, and avoid binges, especially early in treatment or after a dose change.
- Don't skip doses to drink. It doesn't make drinking safer and it weakens your treatment.
- Know the liver warning signs, and don't write off yellow eyes, dark urine, or lasting right-sided pain as a hangover.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking Strattera?**

Many people on Strattera drink occasionally, but the label advises caution and there's no officially safe amount. For a healthy adult who's stable on the drug, one or two drinks now and then may be acceptable, but ask your prescriber first. Avoid alcohol if you have liver problems, high blood pressure or heart disease, low mood, or you're in the first weeks of treatment or a new dose.

**Is atomoxetine bad for your liver with alcohol?**

Atomoxetine carries a warning about rare but serious liver injury, and alcohol adds its own load on the liver. Occasional light drinking isn't known to cause harm in a healthy liver, but regular heavy drinking on a medicine with a liver warning is a real concern. Watch for itching, dark urine, yellow skin or eyes, and pain under the right ribs, and call your doctor if any appear.

**Should I skip my Strattera dose if I'm going to drink?**

Generally no. Strattera works through steady daily use and stays active in your system, so skipping a single dose doesn't make drinking meaningfully safer. It can, however, make your ADHD symptoms worse for a day or two. If you have a big event coming up, ask your prescriber ahead of time instead of adjusting the dose yourself.

**Is Strattera safer with alcohol than Adderall?**

It's different rather than simply safer. Stimulants like Adderall mask how drunk you feel, which leads people to overdrink, and Strattera doesn't do that to the same degree. But Strattera has its own concerns: a liver warning, raised heart rate and blood pressure, and side effects like nausea and dizziness that alcohol can worsen. Neither drug is a green light to drink heavily.

**Why do I feel sick when I drink on Strattera?**

Nausea, upset stomach, dizziness, and reduced appetite are among Strattera's most common side effects, and alcohol causes the same things. Drinking on an empty stomach, which is easy when the drug blunts your appetite, makes it worse. Eat a proper meal first, drink water between drinks, and keep the amount small. If nausea lingers beyond a day, or comes with dark urine or yellow eyes, call your doctor.

**How long after stopping Strattera can I drink normally?**

Atomoxetine usually clears the body within a day or two in most people, though it can take longer in people who process it slowly. There's no officially set waiting period. If you're stopping Strattera, do it with your prescriber's guidance, and if you had any liver or heart issues while on it, ask them before going back to drinking.

**Does DHM help if you drink on Strattera?**

There is no good evidence that DHM reduces Strattera's liver risk or makes it safer to drink on the medication, and its interactions with atomoxetine haven't been studied. DHM has promising research on alcohol metabolism and liver health, mostly from animal studies. If you want to try it, check with your prescriber or pharmacist first, and keep following the advice on drinking lightly.
